Enviro policy expert here.

The 'There were better alternatives' line is kind of misleading. One of main push behind the alternatives wasn't so much their reduced environmental impacts as it was that certain companies held patents on them and the equipment needed to handle them, and these companies were the ones behind much of the CFC production. So there was a financial incentive to phase out the CFC using equipment with the new equipment, and it was one that would benefit the companies who had the financial interest in CFCs. With this factor lining up, there was minimal industry pressure to oppose the new standards, since they'd make a lot of money from a forced upgrade.

Yes, the new chemicals are less reactive, both environmentally and in cooling systems, but the fact that the stakeholders for CFC production were the same people who were stakeholders for CFC replacements made this an unusually easy sell from a policy perspective.

Acid rain wasn't a "scare." It is a real, observable phenomenon that is directly impacted by certain human activity, specifically gaseous nitrogen and sulfur oxides generated by combustion*. But don't take my word for it. Look at the air quality in China and India now. They are having the same issues Europe did starting early in the industrial revolution, and USA did starting in the post WWII manufacturing boom. Europe and USA fixed the problem with NOx/SOx regulations. Before that, shit like this happened: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Smog. People with compromised respiratory systems actually die at a higher rate during periods of heavy smog exposure because they can't handle the increased stress from the acidic air.

I work for a multinational manufacturing company that has factories in USA, Europe, and China. I get sent around to all of them as an auditor on a semi-regular basis.
